title: Applied anatomy: the thyroid, laryngeal nerves and parathyroids

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in the endocrine surgery clinic
brief.scenario: Mrs Joanna Pritchard, 48, has a 4.5 cm right thyroid nodule confined to the gland. Cytology shows papillary carcinoma. Ultrasound shows no abnormal neck nodes. She is listed for total thyroidectomy. Written findings: an anterior view of the neck shows a gland with two lateral lobes joined by a narrow band of tissue lying across the second to fourth tracheal rings. Above the band sits a complete ring of cartilage, and above that a larger shield-shaped cartilage with a midline prominence. An artery descends to the upper pole of each lobe from above; a second artery runs medially from the side, behind the carotid sheath, to reach the back of the lower half of each lobe.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the anatomy of the thyroid, the laryngeal nerves and the parathyroid glands, and relate them to her operation. The examiner will read out further findings as the station goes on.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Gland and vessels, then the two nerves, then the parathyroids, then what to check after surgery.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Tying the inferior thyroid artery trunk before finding the recurrent nerve.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Two lobes and an isthmus, inside pretracheal fascia, so it moves on swallowing."

grid.label: Gland and vessels
grid.fail: Cannot name the lobes, isthmus or arterial supply.
grid.pass: Two lobes joined by an isthmus over the upper trachea, in pretracheal fascia, so it moves on swallowing. Superior thyroid artery (external carotid); inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk).
grid.high: Adds superior, middle and inferior thyroid veins, the middle vein divided early to mobilise the lobe, and a possible pyramidal lobe.

grid.label: Recurrent laryngeal nerve course
grid.fail: Cannot describe how the right and left nerves differ.
grid.pass: Right hooks under the subclavian artery, left under the aortic arch; both ascend near the tracheo-oesophageal groove and enter the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint.
grid.high: Supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid; a right non-recurrent nerve occurs with an aberrant right subclavian artery.

grid.label: Danger points
grid.fail: Ties the inferior thyroid artery trunk laterally without finding the nerve.
grid.pass: The nerve may pass in front of, behind or between branches of the inferior thyroid artery: find it before dividing branches close to the gland.
grid.high: Names the tubercle of Zuckerkandl (nerve usually deep to it) and ligament of Berry as high-risk points; considers intraoperative nerve monitoring.

grid.label: External laryngeal nerve
grid.fail: Does not know the nerve, or confuses it with the recurrent nerve.
grid.pass: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery to cricothyroid; injury lowers pitch and tires the voice.
grid.high: Ligates superior pole branches individually on the capsule; warns voice professionals before consent.

grid.label: Parathyroids
grid.fail: Cannot say where to look for the parathyroids.
grid.pass: Superior (4th pouch): constant, posterior, near the cricothyroid junction. Inferior (3rd pouch): variable, near the lower pole or with the thymus. Mainly supplied by the inferior thyroid artery.
grid.high: Keeps them on their vascular pedicle by capsular dissection; reimplants a devascularised gland into muscle.

grid.label: After surgery
grid.fail: Does not anticipate low calcium or airway problems after total thyroidectomy.
grid.pass: Checks calcium (and parathyroid hormone) after total thyroidectomy; asks about voice; bilateral nerve palsy can cause stridor needing airway support.
grid.high: Warns about tingling and voice change; knows a tense neck haematoma needs the wound opened at the bedside.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Describe the thyroid from the written findings.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's a gland in the neck. I'm not sure which arteries supply it.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How do the two recurrent laryngeal nerves differ?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: They're the same on both sides.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you control the inferior thyroid artery?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Tie the main trunk laterally first to reduce bleeding.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What nerve is at risk at the upper pole?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Somewhere behind the thyroid; I'd just look for them.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What would you check on the ward afterwards?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Two lobes joined by an isthmus over the upper trachea, inside pretracheal fascia, so it moves on swallowing. The superior thyroid artery comes from the external carotid, the inferior from the thyrocervical trunk.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The right hooks under the subclavian artery, the left under the aortic arch. Both ascend near the tracheo-oesophageal groove and enter the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: At the inferior thyroid artery. It can pass in front of, behind or between the branches, so I'd find the nerve before dividing branches close to the gland.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery to cricothyroid. Injury lowers pitch and tires the voice.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The superiors, from the fourth pouch, are constant, posterior near the cricothyroid junction. The inferiors, from the third pouch, vary: near the lower pole or with the thymus. Both mainly depend on the inferior thyroid artery.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Calcium and parathyroid hormone, and her voice. Bilateral nerve palsy can cause stridor needing airway support.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Describe the thyroid and its vessels.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Beyond the arteries, there are superior, middle and inferior veins. I divide the middle vein early to mobilise the lobe, and look for a pyramidal lobe.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What does the recurrent nerve supply?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: All intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid. On the right it may be non-recurrent if there's an aberrant right subclavian artery, so I wouldn't rely on finding it low.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Where is it most at risk?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: At the tubercle of Zuckerkandl, where it usually lies deep to the tubercle, and at the ligament of Berry, where it's closest to the gland. I'd consider intraoperative nerve monitoring.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How do you protect the external laryngeal nerve?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Ligate the superior pole branches individually on the capsule, not en masse. I'd warn a singer or teacher about pitch before consent.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How do you preserve the parathyroids?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Capsular dissection keeps them on their pedicle. If one is devascularised I'd reimplant it into sternocleidomastoid.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What would you tell her about recovery?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: To report tingling round the mouth or fingers and any voice change. A tense swelling in the neck with breathing difficulty needs the wound opened at the bedside.

failures.move: Tying the inferior thyroid artery trunk before finding the nerve.
failures.consequence: Risks dividing the recurrent nerve and devascularising the parathyroids.

failures.move: Mass ligation of the upper pole.
failures.consequence: Can injure the external laryngeal nerve and permanently change her voice.

failures.move: Not checking calcium after total thyroidectomy.
Not knowing the right nerve can be non-recurrent.
failures.consequence: Searches low and divides it higher up.

recovery.line: Two nerves at risk: recurrent at the inferior artery, external laryngeal at the superior artery.

recovery.when: Asked why a total rather than hemithyroidectomy
recovery.line: At 4.5 cm this is T3, and NICE NG230 offers total thyroidectomy for T3 tumours.

knowledge.fact: Recurrent laryngeal nerve: right under subclavian, left under aortic arch; supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.
External laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery to cricothyroid.
Superior parathyroids: fourth pouch, constant. Inferior: third pouch, variable. Main supply: inferior thyroid artery.
NICE NG230: hemithyroidectomy or total for differentiated tumours over 1 cm up to T2 N0 M0; total for T3–T4, N1 or M1.

recall.say: "I find the recurrent nerve before dividing the inferior thyroid artery branches."
recall.trap: Assuming the right nerve always recurs.
recall.finish: Calcium, voice check, watch for haematoma.

sources.name: Gray's Anatomy for Students (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell)
sources.supports: Thyroid lobes, fascia and vessels; course and supply of the recurrent and external laryngeal nerves; parathyroid embryology, position and blood supply

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Thyroidectomy technique: nerve identification, upper pole ligation, parathyroid preservation; postoperative hypocalcaemia, nerve palsy and haematoma

sources.name: NICE guideline NG230: Thyroid cancer: assessment and management
sources.supports: Hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy for differentiated tumours over 1 cm (T1a[m] to T2 N0 M0); total thyroidectomy for T3 or T4, N1, adverse pathology or M1

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; examiner-led questioning in applied knowledge stations

partner.opening: You have the written findings of an anterior view of the thyroid and larynx. Describe the gland and its blood supply.

reveals.finding: Read out: on a posterior view of the right lobe, a thin nerve ascends in the groove between the trachea and the oesophagus, crosses the branches of the artery entering the back of the lower half of the lobe, and passes up behind the joint between the two laryngeal cartilages. What is this nerve, and how does it differ on the left?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the upper pole
reveals.finding: Read out: at the upper pole, a fine nerve runs down alongside the artery entering the upper pole and ends in a small muscle on the front of the ring-shaped cartilage. What is this nerve, and what happens if it is injured?

reveals.trigger: Candidate moves on to the parathyroids
reveals.finding: Read out: the posterior surface of the right lobe is exposed, with the recurrent laryngeal nerve ascending in the tracheo-oesophageal groove. Where would you look for the two parathyroid glands on this side, and what is their blood supply?
Day 1: tingling round the lips; corrected calcium low; voice normal.

push.question: How do the two recurrent nerves differ?
push.expect: Right under subclavian; left under aortic arch.

push.question: Where is the recurrent nerve at risk?
push.expect: Inferior thyroid artery branches; tubercle of Zuckerkandl; ligament of Berry.

push.question: Which nerve is at risk at the upper pole?
push.expect: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve; ligate on the capsule.

push.question: Where are the parathyroids?
push.expect: Superior constant, posterior; inferior variable; inferior thyroid artery supply.

push.question: What would you check after surgery?

curveballs.prompt: The nodule had been 2 cm with no nodes. Would you still do a total?
curveballs.safeAnswer: NICE NG230 offers either hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy for tumours over 1 cm up to T2 N0; a shared decision.

curveballs.prompt: You can't find the recurrent nerve low on the right.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider a non-recurrent nerve with an aberrant subclavian artery; it runs medially straight from the vagus at a higher level.
Possible bilateral recurrent nerve palsy: call the anaesthetist, secure the airway, then laryngoscopy.
